subject: english-language-and-literature
title: English Language and Literature MYP 5 eAssessment Paper B (3 tasks, 80 marks)

questions.content:
[[Q 1.1 | A 3]]
Task 1: Analysing
Questions 1.1 to 1.4 focus on the key concept of communication. Question 1.5 focuses on the key concept of perspective. The criteria assessed are A (Analysing) and B (Organizing). Suggested time for Questions 1.1 to 1.4: 15 minutes. Suggested time for Question 1.5: 35 minutes.

Text A: 'We Are Not Your Weather' (a speech, written for this paper)
This is a transcript of a speech given by a sixteen-year-old student, Tamsin Reyes, to a town council meeting about plans to build on a flood plain beside the river.

Good evening, councillors.

You have a folder in front of you. It is blue, and it is thick, and it contains eleven reports. I have read them all. I would like to tell you what they do not say.

They do not say that on the fourteenth of October the river came up Mill Road in forty minutes. They do not say that my neighbour, Mr Okafor, carried his wife's wheelchair upstairs while the water climbed the stairs behind him. They do not say what a house smells like three weeks after.

You will tell me the plan is safe. You will tell me the drains have been upgraded. You will tell me we cannot stand in the way of progress. Progress. Let us be honest about that word. Progress for whom? Progress to where? A road that leads into a lake is not progress; it is a very expensive way of drowning.

We are not asking for miracles. We are asking you to read the map the river has already drawn. For ten thousand years it has told us where it wants to go. For ten thousand years we have been polite enough to listen. And now, in one meeting, in one folder, you are about to tell it to move.

It will not move.

So I ask you tonight, not as a protest, not as a statistic, but as a neighbour: when the next flood comes, whose name do you want on the page? Because the water will not read your reports. But my generation will.

Thank you.

Text B: a magazine advertisement (written for this paper; in the live exam this would be an image)
[Visual: a full-page photograph taken from above of a suburban street at dusk. Every house is exactly the same grey shape, with identical lit windows. In the centre of the page, one house is painted bright yellow and has a small vegetable garden in front. Soft fog sits at the end of the street. The colours are cold except for the yellow house.]
Headline, large white serif letters across the top: BE THE EXCEPTION.
Sub-headline in smaller italics: Not everything that stands out has to shout.
Body text, small sans-serif font bottom left: At Fernhill Homes we build 40 individual houses on the edge of the Meridian Valley. No two alike. Each with a garden, a view and a story. From £289,000.
Strapline in bold capitals beside a logo of a small tree: GROW WHERE YOU ARE PLANTED.
Website: fernhillhomes.example

Q 1.1 Explain the effect of the repeated structure 'They do not say...' in the paragraph beginning 'They do not say that on the fourteenth of October' in Text A. (3 marks)
questions.mark_scheme: Criterion A, 3 marks. Level 1 (1 mark): identifies the repetition without explaining the effect, e.g. she says 'They do not say' three times. [1] Level 2 (2 marks): describes an effect with some example, e.g. the anaphora builds a list of what is missing from the reports and makes the councillors seem careless. [1] Level 3 (3 marks): explains the effect consistently with precise quotation, e.g. the repeated negative 'They do not say...' contrasts official paperwork with human detail (Mr Okafor, the wheelchair, the smell), building pressure to a climax and making the audience feel guilt as well as sympathy. [1]

questions.content:
[[Q 1.2 | A 2]]
Refer to Text A (printed in Question 1.1). Comment on the speaker's use of the phrase 'a very expensive way of drowning'. (2 marks)
questions.mark_scheme: Criterion A, 2 marks. Level 1 (1 mark): identifies a meaning without development, e.g. the phrase means the plan is a bad idea. [1] Level 2 (2 marks): comments with some explanation, e.g. the sharp, dark metaphor-like phrase turns an economic argument ('expensive') into a life-and-death warning and shows her sarcasm toward the council's idea of progress. [1]

questions.content:
[[Q 1.3 | A 3]]
Refer to Text B (printed in Question 1.1). Analyse the effect of colour and composition in the advertisement. (3 marks)
questions.mark_scheme: Criterion A, 3 marks. Level 1 (1 mark): identifies colour or composition without explaining its effect, e.g. one house is yellow. [1] Level 2 (2 marks): describes an effect with some justification, e.g. the cold grey of the street makes the single yellow house stand out as warm and attractive. [1] Level 3 (3 marks): analyses the effect consistently with precise reference, e.g. the overhead view of identical grey houses suggests dull conformity, and the bright yellow house with the vegetable garden is placed at the centre of the page so readers see themselves as the individual who escapes sameness, which supports the headline 'BE THE EXCEPTION'. [1] Accept the fog, the dusk lighting or the white serif headline as relevant details.

questions.content:
[[Q 1.4 | A 2]]
Refer to Text B (printed in Question 1.1). Describe the purpose of the strapline 'GROW WHERE YOU ARE PLANTED'. (2 marks)
questions.mark_scheme: Criterion A, 2 marks. Level 1 (1 mark): identifies a purpose without explanation, e.g. it is the advert's slogan. [1] Level 2 (2 marks): describes a purpose with an example, e.g. the botanical metaphor, supported by the tree logo, links home ownership to natural growth and stability and ends the advert with a memorable, positive message encouraging readers to commit to the new development. [1]

questions.content:
[[Q 1.5 | A 10 | B 10]]
Refer to Text A and Text B (printed in Question 1.1). Compare and contrast how the two texts present attitudes towards building and the natural environment. (Approximately 350 words) (20 marks)

Criterion A (Analysing) is worth 10 marks and Criterion B (Organizing) is worth 10 marks.
questions.mark_scheme: Criterion A (10 marks) and Criterion B (10 marks), 20 marks in total. Criterion A (10 marks): 9 to 10 marks for effective, perceptive analysis of content, language, structure and technique in both texts with extensive, well-chosen evidence; 6 to 8 for considerable analysis with sufficient, relevant evidence; 3 to 5 for adequate analysis with some evidence; 1 to 2 for limited analysis with few or no examples. Indicative content: Text A (spoken, persuasive, emotive): direct address ('councillors'), anaphora, rule of three ('You will tell me...'), rhetorical questions ('Progress for whom?'), personal anecdote (Mr Okafor), personification of the river ('it wants to go', 'It will not move'), short climactic sentence, closing appeal to the future ('my generation will'). It presents building on the flood plain as dangerous arrogance and respects nature as a force. Text B (visual and written advertising): image of conformity vs individuality, cold/warm colour contrast, imperative headline, minimal body text, price, 'a garden, a view and a story', tree logo and metaphor. It presents nature as a pleasant feature to be sold (gardens, views) and says nothing of risk; the valley setting is a selling point. Contrast: warning vs enticement; community vs individual; collective memory of loss vs aspirational lifestyle; formal and moral register vs light, aspirational register. Similarity: both use emotive appeals and a clear call to the audience. Award up to [10] for Criterion A. Criterion B (10 marks): 9 to 10 marks for effective organisation: clear structure, comparison and contrast sustained throughout, effective linking and a conclusion; 6 to 8 for a considerable degree of organisation with sustained comparison; 3 to 5 for an adequate degree of organisation with some comparison; 1 to 2 for limited organisation, with the texts mostly treated separately. Indicative content: clear introduction with a thesis about the opposing viewpoints; either an integrated or text-by-text structure with explicit comparison; topic sentences; connectives of contrast and similarity; conclusion judging how persuasion differs in speech and advert. Award up to [10] for Criterion B.

questions.content:
[[Q 2.1 | C 10 | D 10]]
Task 2: Producing literary text
This task focuses on the key concept of creativity. The criteria assessed are C (Producing text) and D (Using language).

Image 1 (described in words): a seaside pier at the end of winter. Half the planks are missing and the sea is visible through the gaps. A single deckchair stands upright at the far end, facing the horizon. A flock of starlings wheels above it in a dark spiral.
Image 2 (described in words): a market stall in the early morning. A woman in a patterned headscarf arranges mirrors on a trestle table; each mirror reflects a different part of the street, so that together they make a broken map of the neighbourhood. A cat sleeps beneath the table.

Using one of the images, write a poem or a prose piece that explores memory and the passing of time. You may consider purpose, imagery, mood, structure and voice. State which image you are using before you start. (Approximately 350 words, or a poem of about 20 to 30 lines) (20 marks)
questions.mark_scheme: Criterion C (10 marks): 9 to 10 marks for a high degree of insight and imagination, perceptive stylistic choices and extensive precise detail; 6 to 8 for considerable insight and imagination, thoughtful choices and sufficient detail; 3 to 5 for some insight and imagination, some stylistic choices and some detail; 1 to 2 for limited insight, few stylistic choices and little detail. Indicative content: a named image used as a springboard; a central idea about memory or time developed with symbolism (the pier as ruin, the mirrors as fragments); a consistent voice; structural choices such as stanza shape, repetition or a turn at the end; sensory imagery. A response that uses neither image nor the prompt scores 0 for C. Award up to [10] for Criterion C. Criterion D (10 marks): 9 to 10 marks for an effective range of vocabulary and sentence structures, consistently suitable register and high accuracy with only minor errors; 6 to 8 for a varied range, considerable accuracy and errors that do not hinder communication; 3 to 5 for an adequate range, a degree of accuracy and errors that sometimes hinder communication; 1 to 2 for a limited range, with errors that often hinder communication. Indicative content: figurative language (metaphor, personification), deliberate rhythm, line breaks or sentence length, precise verbs, controlled tone, accuracy appropriate to the form chosen. Award up to [10] for Criterion D.

questions.content:
[[Q 3.1 | B 10 | C 10 | D 10]]
Task 3: Producing non-literary text
This task focuses on the key concept of perspective. You will create a piece of non-literary writing in relation to the global context fairness and development: rights, rules and responsibilities.

The local council in your town plans to close the public library and sell the building for flats. Write a blog post (for a youth community website) arguing for or against the plan. The criteria assessed are B (Organizing), C (Producing text) and D (Using language). (Approximately 350 words) (30 marks)
questions.mark_scheme: Criterion B (10 marks): organisation suited to a blog post: engaging title, short paragraphs with subheadings if wished, a clear sequence of arguments, a call to action, and a personal voice; 9 to 10 effective, 6 to 8 considerable, 3 to 5 adequate, 1 to 2 limited. Award up to [10] for Criterion B. Criterion C (10 marks): perspective on fairness and responsibility shown through insight and relevant detail (access to learning, who benefits, rights of young people, alternatives); 9 to 10 high degree of insight and extensive detail, 6 to 8 considerable, 3 to 5 some, 1 to 2 limited. Award up to [10] for Criterion C. Criterion D (10 marks): chatty but controlled register, persuasive devices (anecdote, rhetorical questions, statistics that are plausible, direct address), varied sentence structures, accurate grammar and punctuation; 9 to 10 high accuracy and effective register, 6 to 8 considerable, 3 to 5 a degree, 1 to 2 minimal. Award up to [10] for Criterion D.
